comments.content:
Splitting the value at the last '=' assumes the `<path>` part of `-proxy=unix:<path>` can never contain '='. But a unix socket is an arbitrary local file path and may legitimately contain '=', e.g. `-proxy=unix:/run/socks=abc`. Here that value is truncated to `unix:/run/socks` and `abc` is treated as a network name:
- if `abc` is not a known network, init fails with a confusing "Unrecognized network" error for what used to be a valid unix path;
- if the trailing segment happens to be a valid network name (`-proxy=unix:/run/socks=ipv4`), the proxy silently points at a different socket path than the one requested.
Note `CheckHostPortOptions` (~line 1224) performs the same truncation for `-proxy`, so validation and the actual parse can also disagree.
Consider detecting a unix socket path on the full value (e.g. `IsUnixSocketPath(param_value)`) before splitting off an `=<network>` suffix, and add a test for a unix socket path containing '='.

comments.content: The help text advertises `tor` as the network name, but everywhere else in the codebase the canonical name is `onion`: `GetNetworkName(NET_ONION)` returns "onion", and `-onlynet` documents `Join(GetNetworkNames(), ...)` which lists "onion". In fact `ParseNetwork()` explicitly deprecates `tor` ("Warning: net name 'tor' is deprecated ... You should use 'onion' instead"), while the new `-proxy` parsing accepts `tor`/`onion` silently. Documenting the deprecated spelling as the primary one is inconsistent and will steer users towards the soon-to-be-removed name.
